description: We are Kepleris, a team interested in space exploration, astronomy, technology, and building creative solutions using data and software. We are looking for enthusiastic team members who enjoy problem-solving, coding, research, data analysis, and working on innovative space-related ideas. We aim to build a practical and engaging solution for the NASA Space Apps Challenge while learning and creating together.
summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky spectral survey into something anyone can watch. You enter a Right Ascension and declination; the tool finds every epoch SPHEREx has imaged that patch, pulls the cutouts from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, re-orients and co-aligns them, and plays them back as a short video — with difference imaging, mean stacking and a per-epoch light curve alongside.

It works for any coordinates and one-click for the five targets named in the challenge, from Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3, across all six detector arrays.

The design is driven by what the data actually does. SPHEREx pixels are 6.2 arcseconds, so a year of motion is often less than one pixel; and cutouts arrive in the spacecraft's orientation, which flipped by ~180° between survey 1 and survey 2. Every frame is therefore resampled north-up and registered by cross-correlation before display. Presets are propagated with Gaia proper motion, because Barnard's Star has moved 4.5 arcminutes since J2000 — almost a whole field — and would otherwise not be in the picture at all.

SPHEREx will image more than a billion objects. Tools like this let volunteers find the ones that move.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool for NASA's SPHEREx all-sky spectral survey. You enter a

patch of sky — right ascension and declination, decimal or sexagesimal — and it finds every

epoch the telescope has imaged there, then plays those epochs back like a short video.

Playback has speed control, a scrubber and frame stepping. Three display modes: Blink (raw

epochs), Difference (each epoch minus a reference epoch) and Mean stack. A detector selector

covers all six arrays from 0.75 to 5.0 microns. Beside the image are the epoch list with

registration quality, a light curve measured in an aperture at the requested position, and

full observation metadata: release, band, exposure, visit count, MJD and Level-2 flag bits.

Every query is a shareable URL. One-click presets cover the five targets named in the

challenge brief.

HOW IT WORKS

1. An IVOA SIA2 query to the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive finds every SPHEREx spectral

image whose footprint covers the position, across Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3.

2. Observations are clustered into epochs using a 32-day window, so the year-long baseline is

not drowned out by near-duplicate frames from consecutive weeks.

3. Each epoch is fetched through IRSA's cutout service and decoded by a FITS reader written

for this project — no astronomy library in the request path.

4. Every frame is resampled to a north-up, east-left grid using the CD matrix from its own

header, then registered to a common grid by masked, high-pass Pearson correlation.

5. Aperture photometry at the requested position produces the light curve; results are cached

so repeat views are instant.

WHAT THE DATA TAUGHT US, AND HOW THE TOOL RESPONDS

- Cutout orientation follows the spacecraft, not the sky: measured at -163.7 degrees in survey

1 and +19.6 degrees in survey 2 at the same field. Blinking the raw arrays shows rotation

that looks like motion, so north-up resampling happens before anything else. This is what

makes the difference mode meaningful.

- A cutout costs about 4 MB regardless of field size, because every file carries a 3.9 MB

exposure-averaged PSF table. The reader skips that extension by size arithmetic, requests a

generous box and bins it down.

- High proper motion moves objects out of the field. Barnard's Star moves 10.3 arcsec per year,

so its J2000 position is about 4.5 arcmin from where SPHEREx sees it in 2026. Presets carry

ESA Gaia DR3 proper motions and are propagated to the observation epoch before searching.

- Bright stars appear as rings: the detectors saturate and the Level-2 products mask the core,

leaving only the wings. Photometry uses a 2.2-pixel aperture to include them, and the

interface explains the artefact instead of hiding it.

- The archive is not always available. IRSA serves roughly two concurrent requests per client

and rejects the rest immediately; the tool retries with backoff and, when a release or a

frame genuinely cannot be retrieved, says so in the interface rather than dropping it silently.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Finding moving objects by comparing images taken at different times is how Pluto was found and

how volunteers have discovered most known comets and brown dwarfs. SPHEREx will image more than

a billion objects every six months, which turns that problem from an evening's work into

something no person can eyeball. A tool that makes "show me what changed here" a one-click

operation — with the alignment and the photometry done properly — lets citizen scientists spend

their time on judgement instead of data wrangling.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

The tool leans on the specific physics of this dataset rather than being a generic image viewer:

sub-pixel registration because the pixels are huge (6.2 arcsec), difference imaging because a

year of motion is often under one pixel, proper-motion propagation because the sky has moved

since the catalogue epoch, and a light-curve panel because two of the five challenge targets are

variables rather than movers. Every view is URL-addressable so a finding can be shared or cited.

TOOLS AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript and React for the interface, Vite for the build, Node for the server-side archive

layer, and a hand-written FITS decoder. No Python, no database and no API keys — IRSA's services

are public. Roughly 2,600 lines written solo in about a day, deployed as a static front end with

serverless functions so the same code serves local development and production.

LIMITS, STATED HONESTLY

One exposure per epoch rather than averaging repeat visits; no spectral extraction from the

LVF axis yet; no Gaia or WISE image overlay yet. Each is a clear next step and none is hidden.
